footer.bottomLine: Manufacturing SMEs · When execution does not take hold

hero.kicker: For managing directors and plant managers in manufacturing SMEs
hero.title: The decision has been made. Why is so little changing in operations?
hero.intro:
The reason is rarely a lack of will. It lies in unclear leadership, unresolved responsibilities, and a lack of alignment at the critical points. That is exactly where I come in.

I work with leadership and directly on the shop floor in manufacturing companies. Not on concepts, but on the question of why execution is not taking hold and what specifically needs to change. Not in the meeting room, but where decisions are meant to have an effect. In leadership situations. In coordination. In operations.

items.title: Execution instead of concept-heavy work
items.text: Change is not planned on top of everything else, but made effective within operations — together with those responsible. With clear structure, clarified responsibilities, and without adding new complexity.

items.title: Clarity in responsibility and alignment
items.text: I do not work with additional programs alongside the organization, but within ongoing operations. Where decisions are made, responsibility is taken, and results emerge.

items.title: Experience from shop floor, leadership, and management
items.text: My perspective is grounded in direct responsibility in operational and leadership roles within industrial environments. It has grown out of accountability in operations and has been sharpened in parallel through study and research.

home.externalReason: Internal knowledge is rarely the problem. What is missing is an assessment without organizational self-interest. Someone who names what everyone senses, but no one internally can say without consequences.

divider.title:
Less abstraction
More operational reality
divider.text: You get the combination of my expertise from different angles: firsthand operational responsibility in manufacturing, academic depth in M&A, cultural integration, and organizational development, and the ability to work directly with leadership and workforce in five languages.

audience.title: Who I work with and when it becomes concrete
audience.subtitle: Typical clients and situations in manufacturing SMEs
targets: Those who have gone through an acquisition and notice that integration is stalling and the cultures are not coming together
Those who have made a decision that is not landing in the organization and no longer know why
Those who have built a new leadership structure that works on paper, but is not actually being practiced
Those who run Lean, but the numbers barely move and leadership is not backing it
Those who, after growth, restructuring, or a leadership change, notice that responsibilities, processes, and accountability no longer fit the new reality
triggers: After an acquisition, cultural tensions arise between old and new structures that no one officially names, but everyone feels operationally
Decisions are made at leadership level, but on the shop floor it is unclear what should change specifically and who is accountable
A cross-site or matrix leadership structure is supposed to work, but responsibilities and decision paths remain permanently unclear
A Lean implementation or continuous improvement initiative has been running for months, but KPIs, leadership behavior, and shop floor routines have still not changed
Formal responsibilities have been redistributed, but in day-to-day operations those who have always decided still decide

orientation.title:
Clarify briefly.
Decide with confidence.
orientation.text:
What remains unresolved comes at a cost: time in coordination loops, energy in leadership friction, and credibility in decisions that do not land.

If you are wondering whether this is your situation right now, we can clarify that in 15 minutes.

services.intro:

Depending on the situation, I work on a one-off basis to create clarity, in a recurring rhythm to provide guidance, or continuously until execution is sustained in day-to-day operations.

approach.title: Approach
approach.intro:
Change rarely fails because of missing concepts. It fails because decisions are not carried, not prioritized, or not executed consistently.

That is exactly where I step in, in the interplay of leadership, prioritization, and execution in ongoing operations.
principles:
Working within ongoing operations:
Clear roles and decision-making and steering rhythms are developed together with leadership so that responsibility can be effectively assumed.

Making impact measurable:
Relevant metrics, standards, and routines are defined together and followed up through leadership and decision-making routines.

Embedding change sustainably:
New ways of working are integrated into routines, collaboration, as well as culture and identity.

how.title: From trigger to execution in three steps
how.subtitle: Not as a concept, but in a way that works in day-to-day operations: clarify together, lead operationally, embed consistently.
how.restriction: This approach is not intended for every situation. It makes sense when it is already clear that change is necessary, but is not taking hold.

steps.text: I understand the starting point, bottlenecks, and dynamics and create the foundation for first robust decisions on target state and priorities.

about.title: About me
about.heroTitle: I know operations, leadership, and the pressure behind them.
intro:
I know these situations not from workshops, but from responsibility.
From production and leadership. From phases in which decisions had to be made under pressure.

Today I work with leaders and organizations in industrial SMEs on exactly these points.
Where change has been decided, but is not taking hold.
Where efficiency, leadership, and corporate culture need to be brought together.
about.profileText:
Acceptance emerges where language, reality, and responsibility fit together.

In M&A, integration, and transformation situations, execution rarely fails because of formal targets, but because of hidden cultural and identity-related tensions. My multilingual access to organizations and my academic work on these dynamics make it possible to surface such tensions early, before they unfold operationally or politically.

My work is grounded in firsthand experience in plant, leadership, and management roles within industrial environments. This leads to a clear approach: change must fit operational reality, be owned by leadership, and be embedded in everyday work.

This is how execution emerges, not as something that needs to be explained, but as something that is carried and lived.

speaking.title: Speaking & Teaching
speaking.intro:
Talks and teaching formats are not a substitute for the actual work. They serve to make connections visible and open up discussion.

I speak about leadership, change, and operational reality. Not from theoretical distance, but from responsibility within the organization.
speaking.topicsHint: Click on a topic for details

topics.title: Efficiency and culture in alignment
topics.subtitle: Why transformation fails and how it succeeds
topics.description: Transformation is not a purely technical process. It is always cultural as well. When strategies fail against lived reality, the reason often lies in the tension between pressure for efficiency and loss of identity. The talk shows how both perspectives can be brought together so that change is not only planned, but understood and carried in everyday work.

topics.title: Shopfloor leadership
topics.subtitle: Leadership through rhythm, not actionism
topics.description: Impact emerges where value creation takes place. When leadership on the shop floor is replaced by short-term actionism, the system loses stability. I show how clear routines, metrics, and a reliable leadership rhythm create orientation and make responsibility effective where problems arise.

topics.title: Lean management
topics.subtitle: Impact in everyday work, not a collection of methods
topics.description: Lean is not a toolbox, but a logic of simplification and learning. Many initiatives fail not because methods are missing, but because they do not connect to everyday work. The session focuses on a few levers that stabilize standards, problem solving, and collaboration without turning into a hunt for methods.

topics.title: M&A integration
topics.subtitle: Culture, identity, and operating model before and after the deal
topics.description: The economic success of mergers is decided after closing, in collaboration, leadership, and identity. Based on practice and research (DBA), I show how questions of culture and identity can be addressed early and how an operating model can emerge that secures performance without losing cultural DNA.

topics.title: Change governance
topics.subtitle: Decide, communicate, embed
topics.description: Change needs a clear framework. Otherwise ambiguity and friction take over. Change governance is the operating system of transformation: decision paths, roles, rhythm, and communication. The talk shows how governance can be built pragmatically so that decisions take hold, communication builds trust, and new ways of working do not fizzle out.

topics.title: Leadership in transition
topics.subtitle: Role, impact, responsibility
topics.description: In transformation phases, expectations of leadership change significantly, away from the pure expert and toward the shaper of orientation, responsibility, and collaboration. I reflect on how leadership remains effective in uncertainty, how roles are clarified, and how responsibility is placed where it actually has an effect in everyday work.
